In [[differential geometry]] and [[gauge theory (mathematics)|gauge theory]], the '''Nahm equations''' are a system of [[ordinary differential equation]]s introduced by [[Werner Nahm]]<ref>{{harv|Nahm|1981}} </ref> in the context of the ''Nahm transform'' &ndash; an alternative to [[Richard S. Ward|Ward]]'s [[Twistor theory|twistor]] construction of [[monopole (mathematics)|monopoles]]. The Nahm equations are formally analogous to the algebraic equations in the [[ADHM construction]] of [[instanton]]s (Nigel Hitchin called them a "bold adaptation"<ref>{{harv|Hitchin|1983}}</ref>), where finite order matrices are replaced by differential operators.

Deep study of the Nahm equations was carried out by [[Nigel Hitchin]] and [[Simon Donaldson]]. Conceptually, the equations arise in the process of infinite-dimensional [[Hyperkähler quotient|hyperkähler reduction]]. They can also be viewed as a [[dimensional reduction]] of the [[Yang–Mills equations#Anti-self-duality equations|anti-self-dual Yang-Mills equations]].<ref>{{harv|Donaldson|1984}}</ref> Among their many applications we can mention: Hitchin's construction of [[Magnetic monopole|monopoles]], where this approach is critical for establishing nonsingularity of [[Bogomolny equations|monopole solutions]]; Donaldson's description of the [[Monopole moduli space|moduli space of monopoles]]; and the existence of [[hyperkähler manifold|hyperkähler structure]] on [[coadjoint orbit]]s of complex [[semisimple Lie group]]s, proved by Kronheimer,<ref>{{harv|Kronheimer|1990}}</ref> Biquard,<ref>{{harv|Biquard|1996}}</ref> and Kovalev.<ref>{{harv|Kovalev|1996}}</ref>

== Equations ==

Let <math>T_1(z), T_2(z), T_3(z)</math> be three matrix-valued meromorphic functions of a complex variable <math>z</math>. The Nahm equations are a system of matrix differential equations

:<math>
\begin{align}
\frac{dT_1}{dz}&=[T_2,T_3]\\[3pt]
\frac{dT_2}{dz}&=[T_3,T_1]\\[3pt]
\frac{dT_3}{dz}&=[T_1,T_2],
\end{align}
</math>

together with certain analyticity properties, reality conditions, and boundary conditions. The three equations can be written concisely using the [[Levi-Civita symbol]], in the form

:<math>\frac{dT_i}{dz}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j,k}\epsilon_{ijk}[T_j,T_k]=\sum_{j,k}\epsilon_{ijk}T_j T_k. </math>

More generally, instead of just considering <math>N \times N </math> matrices, one can consider Nahm's equations with values in a Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>.

=== Additional conditions ===
One often considers the Nahm equations with boundary and reality conditions dependent on the context. 

In the original context of <math>SU(2)</math> monopoles the variable <math>z</math> is restricted to the open interval <math>(0,2)</math>, and the following conditions are imposed:
# <math>T^*_i = -T_i;</math>
# <math>T_i(2-z)=T_i(z)^{T};\,</math>
# <math>T_i</math> can be continued to a meromorphic function of <math>z</math> in a neighborhood of the closed interval <math>[0,2]</math>, analytic outside of <math>0</math> and <math>2</math>, and with simple poles at <math>z = 0</math> and <math>z = 2</math>; and
# At the poles, the residues of <math>T_1, T_2, T_3</math> form the <math>N</math>-dimensional irreducible representation of the group [[SU(2)]].

== Nahm&ndash;Hitchin description of monopoles ==

There is a natural equivalence between 
# the monopoles of charge <math>K</math> for the group <math>SU(2)</math>, modulo gauge transformations, and 
# the solutions of Nahm equations satisfying the additional conditions above, modulo the simultaneous conjugation of <math>T_1, T_2, T_3</math> by the group <math>O(k,R)</math>.

== Lax representation ==

The Nahm equations can be written in the [[Lax form]] as follows. Set

:<math> 
\begin{align}
& A_0=T_1+iT_2, \quad A_1=-2i T_3, \quad A_2=T_1-iT_2 \\[3 pt]
& A(\zeta)=A_0+\zeta A_1+\zeta^2 A_2, \quad B(\zeta)=\frac{1}{2}\frac{dA}{d\zeta}=\frac{1}{2}A_1+\zeta A_2, 
\end{align}
</math>

then the system of Nahm equations is equivalent to the Lax equation

:<math> \frac{dA}{dz}=[A,B]. </math>

As an immediate corollary, we obtain that the spectrum of the matrix <math>A</math> does not depend on <math>z</math>. Therefore, the characteristic equation

:<math> \det(\lambda I+A(\zeta,z))=0, </math>

which determines the so-called '''spectral curve''' in the [[twistor space]] <math>T\mathbb{P}^1</math> is invariant under the flow in <math>z</math>. Moreover, the flow of the ODE linearises on the [[Jacobian variety]] of the spectral curve <ref>{{harv|Griffiths|1985}}</ref>
